items.title: WizSite app: a read-only Canvas page that shows every spec's fleet on one board
items.body:
## Problem

With a few fleets running, the app shows each part of the factory on its own page: what needs you on You, one spec's plan graph on its spec page, and every agent's note on Agents. To see where every agent stands, and which one is waiting on you, you switch between pages and specs.

## Proposal

A new read-only **Canvas** page in the app (`#/canvas`, `#/canvas/<spec>`) that shows every open spec's fleet on one board.

- **One sheet per open spec.** A rail lists the sheets with a coloured block per ticket. An overview (`L`) folds the sheets into an accordion around the open one. Finished specs, and specs with no activity for 3 days, fold into one Quiet sheet, as WizBar does.
- **One stack per ticket**, laid out by the same dagre graph as the spec page, with blocked-by links as lines. The note that holds the claim is in front; behind it are the other notes, the pull request (state, review, checks) and the ticket. A click or Space spreads a stack.
- **One needs-you strip** across the top: the You page's items plus every live `asking` note. A click opens that sheet and highlights the stack.
- **Focus.** Enter on a stack fills the board with that ticket: every note on it, the pull request's facts, what it waits on and what it blocks, with links to GitHub. Esc goes back.
- **Zoom levels.** Close up shows full cards. Zoomed out shows small tiles: only working tickets move, and amber marks what needs you. There is a minimap and `/` to filter by title or number. On a phone the board runs top to bottom, like the spec page.

## What it reads

Only what the app already reads: the specs read and the agents read, through `OW.factory.model()` and `OW.agents.picture()`. A new pure function, `canvasModel(seen, picture, now)`, turns those into sheets, stacks and the strip, with no network or clock of its own, so it can be tested on the app's synthetic fixtures. No new GitHub requests, no new dependency (dagre is already vendored), and no change to OpenWiz or any contract.

## What it doesn't do

- It never writes. Every action is a link to the issue, the pull request, or the decision card on the Queue page.
- It shows no terminal, transcript or CloudRoom state: under the status contract the app reads GitHub, never an agent host.
- Freshness is the app's: agents about every 2 minutes, specs every 10. The page shows how old each read is, and shows partial reads as gaps, never as zeros.

## Plan

Two pull requests to WizSite:

1. `canvasModel()` and the board for one sheet: stacks, blocker lines, the needs-you strip, the route. Proof: tests on the app fixtures that fail first (partial reads, unknown notes, a note that lost its claim), the browser check, and the build-contents check.
2. The sheet rail and overview, spread, focus, zoom levels, the minimap, search, and the phone layout.

The layout and interaction ideas come from ccanvas, an infinite canvas for running many coding agents. Its code is React and wouldn't be copied; the page stays plain JavaScript in the app's style.

## Question

Does a Canvas page fit the app, and is the plan above the right size? I'd build it once you say yes.

## Problem

The WizSite v2 browser test `a spec with a same-origin video plays it on its card, lazily and muted, behind a poster` (`tests/v2/spec-card.test.mjs`) failed once in CI and passed on the next attempt with no code change:

```
AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: in view, the video never loaded
  actual: false, expected: true
```

- Failed run: https://github.com/openwizdev/WizSite/actions/runs/45396352846/attempts/1 (job "Build, links, resources and privacy", step "Test the v2 app records contract and the v2 browser tests"), on WizSite #171, which does not touch the spec card.

A flaky required test fails unrelated pull requests at random, so it is fixed here, not re-run.

## What to build

- Reproduce first: run that test in a loop (for example 50 times in Chromium) and record the failure rate before and after, in the PR.
- Make "in view, the video loads" deterministic: wait on the video's own load or loadeddata event (or the card's lazy-load hook), never a longer fixed sleep.
- Keep the test's strength: a card that never loads its video in view must still fail.

## Owned paths

- `tests/v2/spec-card.test.mjs` in `openwizdev/WizSite`

If the race is in the card itself (`app/`), post the exact line and the smallest diff on this issue and ask for a supporting-edit grant.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The failure reproduces before the fix (loop count and failures recorded), and 0 failures in at least 200 runs after it
- [ ] A card that never loads its video in view still fails the test
- [ ] All WizSite suites pass

items.body:
## Parent

Ticket AP2c of spec #2522 (0.1.2): the write path's follow-ups, part 2 (spec confirmation, audience, record authors). Size: S.

## What to build

Follow-ups from the re-check of WizSite PR #154 at `49f0b712608aad61eceda5bdee91cb98d3ec4a47` (AP2 #2535), logged and merged by the orchestrator's decision. In `openwizdev/WizSite`, each fix proven red first in `tests/v2/records.test.mjs`, and each one's contract text in `contracts/app-records.v1.md`:

- **R15:** a `spec_confirmation` source check fails closed: always `unchecked`, so the app never answers one. decisions.v1's `spec_confirmation` fingerprint covers only the request's own JSON, so there is no trusted spec-body digest to bind to.
- **R16 (privacy):** before sending, read the pinned repository's visibility fresh. If the audience is broader than the preview said, or can't be verified, refuse, and require a new preview and confirm. A restored receipt never reuses its old visibility.
- **R17:** check record authors against a fresh read of the pinned repository's `docs/agents/fleet.md`, never the cached feed. Fail closed when it can't be verified.

This ticket's review is a full review, security included.

## Owned paths

- `app/records.js` in `openwizdev/WizSite`
- `app/data.js` in `openwizdev/WizSite`
- `tests/v2/records.test.mjs` in `openwizdev/WizSite`
- `contracts/app-records.v1.md` in `openwizdev/WizSite` (its source-check, receipts and spec-confirmation text only)

**Relies on:** `app/records.js`

## Links

- #2923 file: `app/records.js`, `tests/v2/records.test.mjs` and `contracts/app-records.v1.md`, which both tickets edit

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] R15, R16 and R17 each fail first at their own assertion, then pass (red commit named in the PR)
- [ ] No `spec_confirmation` is ever current or answerable
- [ ] A repository that turned public, or whose visibility can't be read, refuses the send with zero writes
- [ ] A record author removed after the feed was read is refused at send time
- [ ] All WizSite suites pass with `env -u OPENWIZ_GITHUB_APP_KEY`

## Proof

Spec claims "only the answer and steer forms can be written" and "the token never leaves the browser except to GitHub": `records.test.mjs`, red then green, and the full security review.

items.title: Draft spec: from a feedback report to a landed fix, safely (not approved, nothing built)
items.body:
> **Draft spec for the owner's decision. Nothing here is built or switched on.** It plans no ticket until the owner confirms it. Source: the owner, 2026-11-24, asked for a path from a feedback report to a landed fix that nobody can use to abuse the agents ([private record](https://github.com/jparker2006/ClosedWiz/issues/3065#issuecomment-7129701559)). It builds on the feedback loop (openwizdev/OpenWiz#1838) and its two contracts, and on the report facts of openwizdev/OpenWiz#2955.

## Problem Statement

A user can already file a consented, public report with `/feedback`, and triage can already turn a small, clear one into a ticket. But nothing watches for reports: a person has to ask an agent to look. The moment that becomes automatic, every report is text written by a stranger that an agent reads with no human in between. Someone will try to use that: to give the agents orders, to flood them, to make them spend money, to pull out secrets, or to slip a harmful change in as a "fix".

## Solution

One pipeline of five stages. Each stage has only the powers it needs, and the stranger's words stop at stage 2.

| # | Stage | Who runs it | Sees the report's words | Can write | Holds secrets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Gate** | A script, no model | As bytes to count and hash | Labels on the report | A token for issue labels only |
| 2 | **Read** | A triage model in a closed sandbox | Yes, as quoted data in a file | Nothing: no tools, no network, no `gh` | None |
| 3 | **Write the ticket** | A script, no model | No: only the reader's checked answer | One new issue (the brief), labels, milestone | A token for issues only |
| 4 | **Build and review** | The normal fleet: a builder, a reviewer of another model family, CI, the merge queue | No: the brief only | Its own branch and pull request | A token for that, nothing more |
| 5 | **Tell** | launch-fleet's existing landed comment | No | One fixed-form comment | As today |

The reader's answer is a small JSON object: the contract's six codes, a brief in its own words, the owned paths, and a duplicate number if it sees one. The stage 3 script checks that answer before it writes anything: the shape, the length, that no line of the report was copied, that the brief holds no link, command or code, and that every owned path is outside the guarded list below. A failed check holds the report for the owner. So the only thing that crosses from a stranger to a builder is a short ticket in our words, about paths we allow.

**A switch.** One setting on the default branch, off by default. Every stage reads it first and does nothing when it is off or unreadable.

## Threats and controls

| Threat | Control | Where it is enforced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prompt injection** in the title, body, a comment, an attachment or a link | The reader has no write tool, no network and no secret, so an obeyed order can do nothing. It gets the body as it was at the gate's snapshot, never comments, attachments or linked pages. The report never becomes a ticket body or a builder's prompt: stage 3 rewrites it and refuses a brief that copies a line, a link, a command or code. Text addressed to an agent fails `no_instructions` and holds the report | Sandbox settings; the stage 3 script; the existing triage helper |
| **A poisoned brief** (the reader is talked into asking for something bad in its own words) | Owned paths must be outside the guarded list; one small ticket only; a builder's normal limits; the reviewer judges the change against the brief and the code, never the report; a CI check fails a pull request from a feedback brief that touches a guarded path or goes over the size cap | The stage 3 script; a CI check; review |
| **Spam and floods** | Per author: at most 2 untriaged reports open and 3 a day; over that, later ones are labelled and not read. New or empty accounts (under 30 days old, or no public activity) are never read automatically: held. Whole pipeline: at most 20 reads and 3 started briefs a day. Over 10 reports in an hour trips a breaker: every automatic step pauses and the owner is told once. Duplicates fold: same operation marker, same normalised title and body hash, or the reader names an open report; the duplicate is labelled and linked to the first by the script, and starts nothing | The gate, with no model |
| **Harmful or off-scope requests** (new features, changes to the agents' own rules, other people's projects, anything not a defect in OpenWiz) | Fails `defect` or `no_guarded_change`: held with a reason code, labelled, never started, never answered automatically | The reader's codes; the stage 3 script |
| **Secret or data exfiltration** | No stage that sees the report's words holds a secret or has a network. No stage that holds a secret sees the report's words. Logs are scrubbed by the sender (openwizdev/OpenWiz#2956) and checked again at the gate; a private-looking report is held and never sent to a model. No model-written text is ever posted on a report: the only automatic reply is the fixed landed line | Sandbox settings; the gate; the landed comment's fixed form |
| **Costly runaway work** | A report over 8,000 characters is held unread. One read per report, with a token cap. A brief is size S only. Its builder has a wall-clock cap and a token cap, and gets one fix round; over any cap the work stops, the ticket is held and the owner is told. A daily spend cap for the whole pipeline; reaching it turns the switch off until the next day | The gate; fleet budgets; the stage 3 script |
| **A malicious "fix"** | Unchanged gates: a reviewer of another model family on the exact head, required CI, the merge queue, no direct deploy, and the owner's release instruction and changelog approval before anything ships. Added: the guarded-path and size check above, and a `from-feedback` mark on the pull request so the release notes list every such change | Existing rules; a CI check |
| **Impersonating the owner or the agents** | Identity is the numeric GitHub account id read from the API, never a name, a look-alike login, a signature or a claim in text. Approval never comes from a public report or its comments: only from the owner's own private record. Fleet records, report links, landed comments and facts lines count only from record authors or under their contract's exact form, as today. A report saying it is approved is still a stranger's report | The gate; every existing record check |
| **Edits after triage** | The gate stores the body's hash. An edit after the read changes nothing already written and starts nothing; the report goes back to held | The gate |

**The guarded list** (a brief can never own these; the report is held): agent instructions and skills (`AGENTS.md`, `skills/`, `docs/agents/`), contracts and schemas, `.github/`, CI and release tools, installers, dependency and lock files, anything about credentials, tokens, identity, privacy checks or allowlists, and every file this pipeline itself is made of. A report cannot change the rules its own handling follows.

## Who says yes

| Step | Version 1 (recommended) | Later, only if the owner chooses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Notice a report, gate it, fold duplicates | No human | No human |
| Read it and draft the brief | No human | No human |
| Start the fix | **The owner's yes, one tap per report**, on the drafted brief in the private queue | No human for accounts the owner has vouched for; then for anyone |
| Build, review, CI, merge | No human, as for any approved ticket | Same |
| The landed comment | No human, fixed form | Same |
| Any other public reply | The owner's exact yes, as today | Never automatic |
| Held reports, refusals, anything guarded | The owner | The owner |
| Release | The owner's ship instruction and changelog approval, unchanged | Unchanged |

## The smallest first version

Stages 1 to 3 run by themselves and stop at a **drafted** brief in the owner's private queue, with the reader's codes and the report link. The owner answers yes or no; a yes makes it a normal ready ticket and everything after is the fleet as it is today. Why this first: the owner's tap is about ten seconds, it removes every "starts work with no human" risk while the limits above are tuned on real reports, and it needs no new power: no new token, no new label rule, no change to merge or release. It still delivers the promise: a report is noticed in minutes, and the reporter sees the fix land on their own issue.

Step two, after 20 reports with no bad draft: skip the tap for accounts on a vouched list the owner keeps. Step three, strangers, only on the owner's separate decision.

## Decisions for the owner

One-way decisions are marked. The rest can be changed by a setting.

1. **One-way: a public promise.** Do we say publicly that reports are fixed automatically? Once said, people expect it and attackers aim at it. Recommendation: say "reports are read within minutes and small bugs are fixed quickly", not "automatically".
2. **One-way: strangers start work with no human.** Recommendation: not in version 1; the one tap stays until the vouched list has proven the limits.
3. **One-way: model-written words on a public report under the owner's or the App's name.** Recommendation: never. Only the fixed landed line.
4. **One-way: agent instructions and skills as a target.** Recommendation: guarded forever; a report never changes what agents are told.
5. Which identity stages 1 and 3 use: the OpenWiz App with issues-only permission (recommended), or the owner's login.
6. The numbers: 2 open and 3 a day per author, 30-day accounts, 20 reads and 3 starts a day, the 8,000-character cap, the daily spend cap.
7. Whether refused reports get a visible label (recommended: yes, `needs-triage` plus a reason only in the private queue) and whether refusing is ever answered (recommended: no automatic answer).
8. Release gates stay exactly as they are (recommended; listed so it is a decision and not an assumption).

## User Stories

1. As a reporter, I want my report noticed without anyone asking an agent to look, so that I am not waiting on a person.
2. As a reporter, I want one comment on my issue when the fix merges, so that I know it is done.
3. As the owner, I want a drafted ticket in my queue for each small, clear report, so that one yes starts the fix.
4. As the owner, I want no report to be able to instruct, flood, bill or rob my agents, so that opening this to strangers is safe.
5. As the owner, I want one switch that stops every automatic step, so that I can turn it off in a second.
6. As a builder, I want a brief in the project's own words with paths I may touch, so that I never act on a stranger's text.
7. As a reviewer, I want a pull request from a feedback brief marked as such and checked against the guarded list, so that I know what to distrust.

## Implementation Decisions

- **One new contract** (`feedback-auto.v1`): the switch, the gate's limits and labels, the reader's answer schema, the stage 3 checks, the guarded list, the budgets, and the private queue's draft form. Fixtures for each threat row above, red first.
- **Reuse:** the report, marker, facts line, six codes, brief, report link and landed comment are the existing contracts', unchanged. The gate and stage 3 extend triage's feedback helper; they are scripts with no model call.
- **The reader runs with no tools.** Its sandbox has no `gh`, no network and no credential; it is given two files (the snapshot and a read-only public checkout) and returns one JSON answer.
- **A CI check** fails a pull request that closes a feedback brief and touches a guarded path or exceeds the size cap.
- **Nothing in merge, release or deploy changes.**

## Testing Decisions

Tests feed synthetic reports in and check what comes out: a label, a held note, a drafted brief, or nothing. Each threat row has at least one hostile fixture (an order to the agent, a copied command, a look-alike owner login, a flood, a duplicate, an oversized body, an edit after the read, a brief naming a guarded path). Before the switch is ever turned on, an abuse drill: people the owner invites try to break a copy that points at a throwaway repository.

## Proof

| Claim | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| P1 No stage that sees report words can write or reach a secret | The sandbox settings, and a test that a hostile report's order has no effect |
| P2 A report's words never reach a builder | The stage 3 copy check on fixtures, red first |
| P3 Floods, new accounts and duplicates start nothing | The gate's tests, with no model call counted |
| P4 A brief can never own a guarded path | The stage 3 tests and the CI check's tests |
| P5 Budgets stop work and hold the ticket | Budget tests on a fake fleet |
| P6 Off means off | A test that every stage does nothing with the switch off or unreadable |
| P7 The abuse drill finds no way through | The drill's record, on a throwaway repository |

## Out of Scope

- Building or switching on any of this before the owner confirms the spec.
- Automatic replies in words, automatic releases, and any change to merge or release rules.
- Reading attachments, images, links or comments on a report.
- Feature requests and questions: they stay held for the owner.

items.title: R15 test no longer fails when the spec_confirmation guard is removed (polish for #2924, R1)
items.body:
Follow-up of #2924 (spec #2522)

`tests/v2/records.test.mjs:938` (Standards, test value): the R15 test "spec confirmations are always unchecked and cannot be composed" no longer fails for the R15 bug. The green commit changed the `Net` GraphQL mock to answer `{ data: {} }` instead of a `lastEditedAt`, so the base `app/` also yields unchecked. Deleting the new `|| r.kind === 'spec_confirmation'` guard in `app/records.js` sourceCheck also leaves both R15 tests green: the request falls into the plan-approval branch and fails on the unserved `sub_issues` read. Fix: give the test a world where the guard is the only thing that refuses. For example, serve `GET /repos/acme/factory/issues/41/sub_issues` and an empty `blocked_by`, and set the request's `tickets` and `fingerprint` to the revision-v2 digest. That way removing the guard turns the result into `matched`. Found in pull request openwizdev/WizSite#191 at 1f5da4ff4a48fa462b0834cfcb8141341bb4eb0f; it is polish and did not block the merge.

items.title: 0.2.0 spec: drivers live in their own repositories
items.body:
## Problem Statement

Every driver lives inside OpenWiz today, in `adapters/`. Fifteen non-core drivers are merged or waiting in about thirty open pull requests, and each one adds rows to the kernel's CI, release list, import paths and key-host registry. So the kernel keeps growing with every host, every driver change waits on OpenWiz's own review and release, and an outside author cannot ship a driver for their own host without a pull request to OpenWiz. Users get a new driver only when a whole kernel release ships.

## Solution

OpenWiz keeps a small kernel with two core drivers: `local` (your own computer or server) and `boat` (boat.dev, the one cloud default). Every other driver lives in its own public repository, made from one template, and is listed in WizMarket. When you pick a host that is not core, OpenWiz finds it in WizMarket, downloads the exact version the listing pins, checks its checksum and its kit receipt, shows you what it is, and installs it after one yes. Drivers OpenWiz itself publishes, such as CloudRoom, are pinned by each kernel release, so picking them needs no extra click and existing users keep working after an update with no click at all. An outside author forks the template, builds, runs the five-check kit, and opens one pull request to WizMarket: OpenWiz itself is never touched.

## Changelog headline

Anyone can now ship an OpenWiz driver from their own repository: pick any host in WizMarket and OpenWiz fetches, checks and installs it for you.

## User Stories

1. As a new user, I want to pick "this computer" or boat.dev during setup and have it work with nothing fetched, so that the first fleet starts as fast as today.
2. As a new user, I want to pick CloudRoom (or another driver OpenWiz publishes) with the same single choice, so that a moved driver costs me no extra click.
3. As a user, I want OpenWiz to show me a driver's name, publisher, version, where its login lives, and whether and when it passed the kit, before any of its code runs, so that I know what I am saying yes to.
4. As a user, I want an unverified driver to need its own explicit yes after a plain warning, so that nothing unproven runs on my machine without my word.
5. As a user, I want a driver whose download does not match its pinned checksum, version or files to be refused with a plain next step, so that a tampered or moved release never runs.
6. As an existing user on CloudRoom, I want `openwiz update` to fetch the CloudRoom driver before it switches builds, and to keep my last good build if that fails, so that updating never leaves me without a host.
7. As an existing user, I want my settings, Roster and host names to stay exactly as they are, so that nothing I configured changes.
8. As a user of OpenWiz 0.1.1 or earlier, I want my installed build to keep its bundled drivers, so that the move changes nothing until I update.
9. As a user, I want a new verified version of a driver I already approved, from the same repository and publisher, to arrive on update with a one-line notice, and anything else (another repository, another publisher, or no longer verified) to ask me again.
10. As an outside driver author, I want a `driver-template` repository I can use as a template or fork, with the driver, its tests, its CI and its release already wired, so that I start from a driver that already passes the kit on fixtures.
11. As an outside author, I want my repository's CI to run my driver's tests and the kit on fixtures on every pull request, with no secrets, so that I know it is right before I spend a live run.
12. As an outside author, I want one command to run the five checks on my real host, write the receipt for my release's exact commit, attach it to the release and open my WizMarket pull request with my own GitHub login after my yes, so that publishing is one step.
13. As an outside author of a host that takes an API key, I want my listing to carry the host's address and key names for the user to approve, so that I never need an OpenWiz pull request (subject to the owner's key-host rule below).
14. As a WizMarket reviewer, I want the check to refuse a verified driver listing whose receipt is not for the listing's pinned commit, or whose package fields are malformed, so that verified always means this exact release passed.
15. As the owner, I want each kernel release to package only the core drivers, so that the kernel stays tiny and a driver fix ships without a kernel release.
16. As the owner, I want each kernel release to pin the drivers OpenWiz publishes by version and checksum, so that what existing users get on update is reviewed with the release.
17. As a driver's builder with an open pull request on OpenWiz, I want my commits, authorship and review state to move with the driver to its new repository, so that no work or approval is lost.
18. As a reviewer, I want a verdict given at a pull request head to carry to the moved pull request when the driver's files are byte-identical, so that only the new packaging and CI files need a fresh look.
19. As the fleet, I want a pending live check to run against the driver's new release and produce its WizMarket receipt, so that the holds clear the same way they would have.
20. As a user of a harness row (Goose, Gemini CLI and the rest), I want rows to keep working through the local driver unchanged, so that the move does not touch them.
21. As the release owner, I want nothing in this move to touch the 0.1.1 release branch or its sealed candidate, so that 0.1.1 ships as sealed.
22. As the operator of the live-check rig, I want the rig to run a driver from its installed folder or a release, not only from `adapters/`, so that moved drivers can still be live-checked.
23. As a user of the write-driver skill, I want it to start my driver from the template in my own repository and end at a WizMarket pull request, so that I never touch OpenWiz.
24. As a visitor to openwiz.dev, I want each driver's page to link its own repository and say whether it is verified, so that I can see where it lives.

## Implementation Decisions

**Core drivers.** The kernel keeps `local` and `boat`. boat.dev is the cloud default because it is already verified on its real host in WizMarket, it is the owner's chosen next cloud host for the fleet, its driver uses the host's own signed-in CLI with no key helper, and it is the cheapest cloud sandbox in the compute research. CloudRoom stays a first-party driver that setup still offers with one choice, through the release pin below; it is only listed (not yet verified) in WizMarket today, and OpenWiz is moving off CloudRoom as its control plane. The CloudRoom pieces that are not a driver (the `room-cli` allowlist behind `openwiz ls`, `show` and `fleet`, and setup's CloudRoom installer) stay where they are in this spec.

**Harness rows stay.** A harness row is data read by the core local driver, never run as code. Rows stay with the local driver, and the open row pull requests continue as they are.

**Repositories.** First-party drivers live at `openwizdev/driver-<name>`, where `<name>` is the name the driver's `version` answer gives. A new listing uses that name as its WizMarket id; a driver already listed keeps its id (for example `cursor-cloud-agents`), and its package block names the driver. The template is `openwizdev/driver-template`, marked as a GitHub template repository. Outside authors may use any repository name; the template recommends `<owner>/openwiz-driver-<name>`. The spec names these repositories and creates none: each is created by its own ticket, the pilot first.

| Repository | Driver | Comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openwizdev/driver-template` | the template | `adapters/template` |
| `openwizdev/driver-openclaw` | OpenClaw (the pilot) | `adapters/openclaw`, and its open effort pull request |
| `openwizdev/driver-cloudroom` | CloudRoom | `adapters/cloudroom` |
| `openwizdev/driver-devin` | Devin | `adapters/devin` |
| `openwizdev/driver-hermes`, `driver-factory`, `driver-pane`, `driver-codespaces`, `driver-sprites` | Hermes, Factory, Pane, GitHub Codespaces, Fly Sprites | their open pull requests |
| `openwizdev/driver-conductor`, `driver-cursor`, `driver-warp-oz`, `driver-openhands`, `driver-capy`, `driver-tembo`, `driver-ona` | the key-host drivers | their open pull requests |

**The driver package contract** (new, kernel, contract-first). One versioned contract fixes: the repository layout a driver repository keeps (the driver program, `schema.json` byte-identical to the kit's, its README with the login and effort lines, its tests and fixtures); release tags `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>`; the release assets (one archive holding only the files a user needs, a manifest naming the driver's name, version, driver contract version, kit commit and every file's hash, and a checksums file, plus the receipt once a live run passes); the listing's package block (repository, version, full commit, asset URL, archive checksum, kit commit) and an optional key-host block; the install folder layout; the trust and update rules below; and the first-party pin file a kernel release carries. Synthetic fixtures cover a good package and each broken one.

**WizMarket listing v2.** Listing v1 never changes, so a listing v2 is added beside it. A v2 driver or harness listing carries the package block. The check refuses a v2 listing whose package block is malformed, whose asset is not a release asset of the listed repository, or which is `verified` with a receipt whose driver line is not the package's repository and commit. The index gains the v2 fields; v1 listings read as before.

**Finding and fetching a driver.** The installer resolves a host name in this order: a core driver in the installed build; a first-party pin in the build's pin file; a WizMarket listing, read from WizMarket's `main` at one commit it records. It downloads only the archive at the listing's or pin's asset URL, over HTTPS, from that repository's GitHub releases, follows no redirect off GitHub, and checks the archive's checksum, then every member against the manifest by the same strict archive rules as the kernel's own install (no links, no extra or missing file, exact modes), then that the driver's name and `schema.json` match. Nothing from the archive runs before all of that and the yes.

**The yes.** Picking a core driver or a first-party pin in setup or settings is the yes. A verified WizMarket driver shows one confirmation with its name, publisher, version, login line, what it can do and its receipt date, and installs on yes. A listed (unverified) driver shows a plain warning that it has not passed the kit and needs its own explicit yes. Agents never answer it for the user. The approval is saved per driver as repository, publisher, version and checksum.

**Install folder.** Fetched drivers are installed, owner-only, into one drivers folder of the install that also holds the core drivers (copied from the verified build and checked against its manifest whenever the folder is rebuilt), laid out `<name>/driver`. launch-fleet's existing `$OPENWIZ_ADAPTERS/<host>/driver` call stays unchanged. The one WizSkills change: the install skill points `OPENWIZ_ADAPTERS` at this folder instead of the build's own runtime folder, and resolves a picked host that is not core through the kernel's fetcher. That ships in a WizSkills release and a new pin, whose tag is the owner's word as usual.

**Updates.** On `openwiz update`, each approved driver moves to its listing's newer version only when the repository and publisher are unchanged and the new version is verified; it says so in one line. Any other change asks again. A driver that the new build stops bundling and that its pin file names is fetched before the build switches; if that fails, the last good build stays selected and the user is told the next step.

**Kit in each driver repository.** The template's CI, on every pull request, runs the driver's own tests and the kit on fixtures (the fake harness and a local tracker file), at an OpenWiz kit commit pinned in the repository, with no secrets and read-only permissions. A tag runs the release workflow, which builds the package and its checksums. The live run stays the author's: the template's receipt tool runs the five checks on the real host from the author's own machine and logins, writes the 14-line receipt for the release's exact commit, attaches it to the release, and opens the WizMarket pull request with the author's own `gh` after their yes. WizMarket's review stays the gate, as in listing v1.

**Key hosts (needs the owner's yes, a person's ticket).** Recommendation: a listing's key-host block carries the host's HTTPS address, the environment variable and the keychain entry; the user's yes approves them with the driver; the key helper reads the kernel's registry plus the approved entries of installed drivers; an entry whose variable or keychain entry another host already uses is refused; and the kit can take a driver repository's own registry entry on its loopback key check. This moves the address review from OpenWiz to WizMarket plus the user's yes, so it waits for the owner. Until then the key-host drivers do not move.

**Releases.** A kernel release packages only the core drivers, the kit files the kit's checks need, the fetcher and the pin file. A driver enters the pin file only with a verified receipt for that exact commit, or as a byte-identical carry-over of a driver the previous release bundled (so CloudRoom users are covered before CloudRoom's own receipt). The release gates check the pin file's hashes. Non-core drivers leave the release's driver list, CI, import paths and the kernel's docs.

**Moving open pull requests.** One ticket per driver. It creates the repository from the template and imports the driver's history: for a merged driver, its folder's commits from OpenWiz `main`; for an open pull request, that branch's commits for the driver's folder, so commits and authorship survive. The pull request's kernel-side changes (CI row, release list, import paths, key-host row) are dropped, since the kernel no longer lists the driver. It opens the driver's first pull request in the new repository, then comments on the old pull request with the new link, the last verdict and the head it was given at, and closes it unmerged. A verdict at that head carries over when the driver's files are byte-identical to that head; the reviewer then checks only the new repository's CI and packaging files. Any difference gets a re-check of the difference. The old ticket and any pending live-check ticket get a comment naming the new repository and release; the planner re-points them. A live check then runs on the new release and its receipt goes to WizMarket. Drivers moved this way keep their WizMarket listing id, updated to v2 with the new repository.

**Order.** The contract first; then WizMarket v2, the fetcher and the template side by side; then the pilot, OpenClaw, from its own repository to a verified receipt; then, after 0.1.1 is published, the install wiring and OpenClaw leaving the kernel; then a live check of the whole pilot path on a clean Linux machine. Only after that pilot passes do the other drivers move, side by side: the five without a key first, the key-host ones after the owner's key-host rule, CloudRoom and Devin last, then one kernel clean-up. OpenClaw is the pilot because it is merged and verified, its login stays on the user's machine with no key or cloud spend, no release has bundled it, and it has one open pull request to practise the move on.

**0.1.1 stays untouched.** Nothing here writes to the `release-0.1.1` branch or its sealed candidate. The 0.1.1 build reads nothing from OpenWiz `main` or WizMarket. Any change on `main` to a file that `release-0.1.1` also carries (the drivers it bundles, the kit, the install and release tools and their contracts) waits for the 0.1.1 release ticket to finish; new repositories, new files and WizMarket work may start before.

## Testing Decisions

Good tests check behaviour from the outside: a fetch is checked by what it installs or refuses, a listing by what the WizMarket check prints, a release by the archive it builds. Everything runs on synthetic fixtures and fake `gh` and fake GitHub release servers, with no network.

Seams:

- **The fetcher's command line**, against a fake GitHub release server and fixture packages: good, wrong checksum, extra file, link, wrong name, wrong schema, redirect off GitHub, unverified without the extra yes, and update with a changed publisher. Prior art: the kernel install's archive tests.
- **WizMarket's check and index**, on v2 fixtures beside the v1 ones. Prior art: WizMarket's own check tests.
- **The template repository's CI**, which must pass on the template and fail on a planted break. Prior art: the kit's own tests with the template and planted drivers.
- **The release build**, which must list only the core drivers and the pin file, and refuse a pin whose hash does not match. Prior art: the release package tests.
- **The update path**, on a fixture install with CloudRoom active.

## Proof

| Claim | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| P1 A fetched driver runs only after its checksum, manifest, name and schema match and the user said yes; every broken fixture is refused | Fetcher tests, red first |
| P2 WizMarket refuses a verified v2 driver listing whose receipt is not for its pinned commit, and v1 listings read as before | WizMarket check tests, red first |
| P3 A repository made from the template passes its own CI, and a planted break fails it | The template's CI runs, green and red |
| P4 OpenClaw from its own repository passes 5 of 5 on its real host, and its receipt is merged in WizMarket | The receipt and its WizMarket pull request |
| P5 A kernel build carries only the core drivers and a pin file whose hashes match | Release tests, red first |
| P6 Updating an install that uses CloudRoom fetches the pinned driver first, and keeps the last good build when that fails | Update tests, red first |
| P7 Every moved driver keeps its commits and authorship, and its old pull request links the new one with its review state | Review of each move |
| P8 On a clean Linux machine, picking OpenClaw fetches, verifies and installs it after one yes, and the kit passes through the installed driver | The live check below |

## Live check

On a clean Linux machine (the owner's PC or the new server), install the build from `main` after the pilot lands, pick OpenClaw as a host, say yes once, and run the kit through the installed driver on a throwaway ticket. Then tamper with one byte of a copy of the release and show the fetch refuses it. Size: one run, about 20 minutes, no cloud spend. The owner's part: start it, and say yes once at the confirmation.

## Out of Scope

- Moving harness rows out of the local driver (a later spec may add row packages through WizMarket).
- Moving the non-driver CloudRoom pieces (the `room-cli` allowlist and setup's CloudRoom installer).
- Paid listings, accounts or a WizMarket server.
- Any change to the 0.1.1 release branch or its candidate.
- Choosing tools for the user automatically from WizMarket (the 0.03 direction).
- The app's settings screen for picking a host: the 0.2.0 settings work calls this spec's fetcher; this spec builds the command it calls.

## Further Notes

- Decided by Jake on 2026-11-24, as a one-way door on the 0.2.0 map: the kernel keeps only the core drivers (`local` and at most one cloud default), and every other driver moves to its own repository, listed in WizMarket and verified by the five-check kit, to make room for outside driver authors. [Private record](https://github.com/jparker2006/ClosedWiz/issues/3197#issuecomment-7131036237).
- Principles this spec follows: the kernel stays small; users make as few clicks as possible; outside authors can publish a driver without changing OpenWiz.
- Builds on the driver contract (driver v1, its kit and key helper), the WizMarket listing contract (listing v1) and the install contract.
- Builders: Gemini 4 Neon at medium effort through Antigravity. Reviewers: Claude Opus 5.5 at medium effort.
- Recommended for the owner: boat.dev as the one cloud default; OpenClaw as the pilot; the key-host rule above.

items.title: 0.1.2 spec: Local first, capped overflow
items.body:
## Problem Statement

A user with a server of their own wants their builders to run there first, because it is already paid for, and to go to a cloud sandbox only when the server is full. OpenWiz can't do that today. `docs/agents/host.md` names exactly one host (records v1, section 6). A Roster start never tries a second entry (roster v1, pick rule 4). No driver can say it is full: the local driver takes as many runs as it is given, and driver v1's only refusal is a generic error. Everything goes to one place. Either the server gets overloaded, or every builder pays for a sandbox.

## Solution

Local first, capped overflow. A project lists its hosts in the order it prefers them, `Host: local, boat`. Each host has an optional cap on how many agents run there at once, set on the machine that runs its driver. A driver at its cap answers with one new, exact "full" refusal and starts nothing. launch-fleet takes that answer as a signal, not a failure: it tries the next host in order. When every host is full, the start waits for the fleet's next wake. Nothing is reported as failed, and no retries burn. A wake or stop always goes back to the run's own host, as today (records v1, H2). With a Roster, the same spill-over runs down the Roster's candidates in table order.

## Changelog headline

Run your builders on your own server first, and send only the overflow to a cloud sandbox, up to a cap you set.

## User Stories

1. As a user with a server, I write `Host: local, boat`, and new builders start on my server until it is full, then on boat.dev.
2. As a user, I set how many agents may run at once on each host, on that host's machine (`OPENWIZ_LOCAL_MAX`, `OPENWIZ_BOAT_MAX`). With no cap set, a host behaves exactly as it does today.
3. As a user, I set a cap on the overflow host, and it is never passed. When the base and the overflow are both full, the next start waits and goes ahead on the fleet's next wake. It isn't reported as a failed start.
4. As a user, a builder I started on my server is always woken and stopped there, even after it filled up or my host list changed.
5. As a user with a Roster, the same spill-over follows my Roster's table order: a host entry that answers full gives the start to the next candidate for that role.
6. As a driver author, I can make any driver say "full" with one fixed refusal, and every caller that predates this work still reads it as an ordinary refusal.
7. As a user with only `Host: local` or no host file, nothing changes.

## Implementation Decisions

- **The full refusal (driver v1, new section "Full").** A driver that can't take one more run refuses `start` under D3 (exit 1) and starts nothing. Its `next` is exactly `this host is full: start on the next host, or wait for a free place`, and its `error` says how many agents are running and the cap, such as `local is full: 2 of 2 agents are running`. There is no new `can` entry and no schema change, so `kernel/driver-kit/schema.json` and every driver's `schema.json` stay byte for byte as they are. A caller that predates this sees an ordinary refusal. Only `start` answers full. `wake` and `stop` are never refused as full: a wake must reach its own run (D5). The section adds this rule and changes no other v1 rule.
- **The ordered host setting (records v1, section 6).** The one setting line may name one or more hosts, separated by commas, in the order they are preferred: `Host: local, boat`. Each name keeps today's form, no name appears twice, and there are at most 8. H1, H2 and H4 are unchanged. H3 changes in one way: a line that breaks this form starts nothing. A start tries each host in order. A `full` answer moves on to the next host, and any other refusal stops there, as today. When every host answers full, the start waits. Caps are never written in the repository (H4): they are a fact about a machine.
- **The Roster's spill-over (roster v1, pick rule 4).** A picked entry whose driver answers full isn't a failed start: the next candidate in table order is tried. Any other refusal is retried and reported as today, and the next candidate is never tried in its place. When every candidate answers full, the start waits, and the fleet says exactly `roster: every entry for the <R> role is full; the start waits`. New fixtures: `full/` (the first entry full, the second picked), `all-full/` (a wait) and `full-then-failed/` (a failure after a full answer is reported as a failure and isn't passed on).
- **The local driver's cap.** `OPENWIZ_LOCAL_MAX` is a whole number from 1 to 1000; unset means no cap. A run counts while it is starting or while its last turn is running. A run whose turn ended and is waiting for a wake doesn't count. The count and the start's save happen under one driver-wide lock, so two starts at once never both take the last place. A bad value is refused under D3, and nothing starts.
- **The boat driver's cap.** `OPENWIZ_BOAT_MAX`, read the same way. A run counts while it is starting, or while boat shows its sandbox as not stopped (boat's own idle auto-stop frees the place). An unreadable count answers full, never "go ahead". boat's own refusal at its plan's limit on concurrent sandboxes also answers full, and its start-rate limit answers full too, because boat never queues a start.
- **launch-fleet's `host.py`.** `which` prints the ordered list. `start` tries the hosts in order and saves the run with the host that took it. All full is a new outcome, `waits: every host is full (<hosts>); the start is tried again on the next wake`, on exit 1, with no failure note, no failure comment and no retries. The fleet's next wake starts the ticket again, as it would any ready ticket without a run. Only start answers move on to the next host.
- **Contract-first tickets:** LF1 (driver v1 and records v1) and LF2 (roster v1) are docs and fixtures only. The exact refusal text and host-line form above are fixed here, so both run in parallel and the drivers build against LF1.

## Testing Decisions

- **Seam 1: each driver on its fixtures.** `adapters/local/test_driver.py` and `adapters/boat/test_driver.py`, red first. With the cap at N, start N+1 runs: the last answers the exact full refusal and starts nothing. A finished turn frees its place. A wake at the cap still runs. Two starts at once at N-1 take one place between them. Unset keeps today's behaviour. The kit's five checks still pass unchanged.
- **Seam 2: `host.py` on fake drivers.** `test-host.py`: `local` full, so `boat` takes it and the run is saved on `boat`; both full is a wait, with no comment and no note; a non-full refusal on `local` never tries `boat`; a one-host line works as today; a malformed list starts nothing.
- **Seam 3: the Roster reference reader.** `cargo test -p openwiz-tests --test cli-agent roster_contract` runs the new fixtures. WizSkills' Roster pick runs the same cases.
- **Prior art:** driver v1's effort refusal (an exact `next` text that callers read), `host.py`'s retry and report for failed starts (#1446), and the boat driver's limit handling.

## Proof

- **P1** (contracts): LF1 and LF2 are reviewed against this spec, and the Roster fixtures pass the reference reader.
- **P2** (drivers): the local and boat fixture tests show the cap, the full refusal and the free place on a finished turn, red first.
- **P3** (routing): `test-host.py` shows the order, the spill-over, the all-full wait and the saved host, red first.
- **P4** (live): on the owner's server, the live check in LF7.

## Checkpoints

- One-way door: yes
- User-visible: yes

## Live check

LF7, by a person, because a boat sandbox costs money. On the user's own server, set `Host: local, boat` on a throwaway repository, with `OPENWIZ_LOCAL_MAX=2` and `OPENWIZ_BOAT_MAX=1`, and start four throwaway tickets. Expected: two start on `local`, one on `boat`, and the fourth waits. When one local builder finishes, the next wake starts the fourth on `local`. Record which host started each run, the waits, and the exact heads.

## Out of Scope

- A base of several machines: a pool driver that runs the local driver over `ssh` on the least-loaded machine. That is a later spec.
- A daily credit or spend cap on the overflow host. None by default.
- Setup asking for a host list or caps (the install's first fleet writes one host as today), and the app showing load per host.
- Moving a running agent between hosts.
- Drivers other than `local` and `boat` adopting the cap. Any driver can adopt it later under LF1's rule.

## Further Notes

The owner approved this plan on 2026-11-24: local first, with a capped overflow ([private record](https://github.com/jparker2006/ClosedWiz/issues/3065#issuecomment-7131254129)). It builds on an earlier confirmed decision: own machines first, cloud only when they're full, no credit cap by default. The cap sizes come from a separate CPU measure on the server.

items.title: spec: openwiz.dev/book, our own booking page for the team call
items.body:
## What

`openwiz.dev/book`: OpenWiz's own booking page for the 30-minute team call. A visitor picks a free 30-minute slot, enters a name, an email and one line about their team, and books. It replaces the third-party booking link on `/team`, which stays as it is until the maintainer says to switch. The page installs as a progressive web app.

## Why

The third-party booking page cannot be installed as an app and does not look like OpenWiz. The call is the site's one buy button, so it should be ours, in the OpenWiz design.

## Design defaults (stated, changeable by environment setting)

- **Busy time:** the maintainer's Google Calendar, read from the calendar's secret iCal address (`BOOK_ICAL_URL`), or from Google's free/busy API when Google credentials are set. A calendar that cannot be read offers no slots (fail closed).
- **Hours:** Monday to Friday, 11:00 to 18:00 Pacific; 30-minute slots on the half hour; 15 minutes clear on each side of every busy event and booking; at least 4 hours' notice; at most 14 days ahead; at most 4 calls a day.
- **Storage:** Cloudflare D1, in the database the site already has bound (`BOOK_DB`, falling back to the existing binding), tables prefixed `book_`.
- **Calendar write:** when Google credentials exist, a booking is also written to the maintainer's Google Calendar. Best effort: a failed write never loses a booking.
- **Email:** Resend (`RESEND_API_KEY`), from `BOOK_FROM`. The visitor gets a fixed-template confirmation with a calendar file and a cancel link; the maintainer gets a notice with the visitor's details.
- **Abuse:** same-origin JSON only, a honeypot field, per-visitor and global rate limits, bookings only for a slot the server itself offers, and no visitor-typed text in the email sent to the visitor's address (no open relay).
- **Switch:** `BOOK_MODE` is `off` (default: the API answers unavailable and the page says so), `fake` (a built-in fake calendar, for previews and tests) or `live`.
- **No price or payment** on the page.
- **Private view:** a token-guarded feed (`BOOK_FEED_TOKEN`) lists bookings for the maintainer's own calendar view.

## The contract (`openwiz.book.v1`)

All answers are JSON with `Cache-Control: no-store`. Errors are `{"error": "<code>", "message": "<plain sentence>"}`.

- `GET /api/book/slots` → `200 {"schema":"openwiz.book.v1","mode":"live"|"fake","timezone":"America/Los_Angeles","minutes":30,"slots":["2026-11-25T19:00:00Z", ...]}` (UTC, ascending). `503 unavailable` when the mode is off, settings are missing or the calendar cannot be read. `429 rate_limited`.
- `POST /api/book` with `{"start","name","email","team","website","tz"}` (`website` is the honeypot and must be empty; `tz` is the visitor's IANA zone, used only for the email's wording) → `200 {"ok":true,"booking":{"id","start","end"},"email":"sent"|"skipped"|"failed"}`. `400 bad_request`, `409 slot_taken`, `429 rate_limited`, `503 unavailable`. A filled honeypot gets the same `200` shape and nothing is stored or sent.
- `POST /api/book/cancel` with `{"id","token"}` → `200 {"ok":true}`; `404 not_found` for anything else. Idempotent.
- `GET /api/book/feed` with `Authorization: Bearer <BOOK_FEED_TOKEN>` → `200 {"schema":"openwiz.book.v1","bookings":[{"id","start","end","name","email","team","status":"booked"|"cancelled","created"}]}` from 7 days back to the horizon. `404` when no token is set, `401` when it does not match (constant-time compare).

Limits: `name` 1 to 80 characters, `email` one address up to 254, `team` 1 to 200, no control characters; request body at most 4 KB.

## Out of scope

Switching the `/team` link, deploying the page, payments, rescheduling (cancel and rebook), several call types.

## Proof

Each ticket's tests green in WizSite CI; a local end-to-end run in fake mode with screenshots at phone and desktop width; the maintainer's go before any merge to `main` (a merge deploys the site).

items.title: 0.1.2 spec: App v2, one queue to answer decisions and steer specs
items.body:
## Problem Statement

openwiz.dev/app shows what needs you, but it can't act. To answer a decision or steer a spec, the owner leaves the app and says it in chat. On a phone, that turns a one-tap decision into a context switch.

## Solution

v2 turns the app's "Needs you" into one queue with two kinds of card:

- **A decision to answer.** The card shows the request and its Rec, with one tap for yes, one for no, or a typed reply.
- **A spec to watch and steer.** The card plays the spec's video when it has one, and shows its plan picture otherwise. It has three buttons: Ship it, Change something and Not now.

Each answer or steer is a GitHub comment the app writes as the signed-in user, through their own GitHub sign-in, in the record form the fleets and the orchestrator already read. There is no backend: every write goes through one small records layer in the browser, so a later change of records home touches one place. Before anything is posted, a dry run shows the exact comment.

v2 proves itself in the owner's own room first, behind a switch that is off by default, then turns on for everyone at openwiz.dev/app.

## Changelog headline

Answer decisions and steer specs from one queue in the app.

## User Stories

1. As the owner, I open the app and see one queue holding both the decisions that need me and the specs I can steer.
2. As the owner, I answer a decision with one tap on yes, one on no, or a typed reply.
3. As the owner, I watch a spec's video on its card (or see its plan picture when there is no video), then tap Ship it, Change something or Not now.
4. As the owner, I see the exact comment before it is posted, and I post it or cancel it.
5. As the owner, my answer lands as a comment from my own GitHub login, in the form the orchestrator reads, on the request's own issue or pull request.
6. As a user, my GitHub sign-in token stays in my browser: no OpenWiz server stores it, and the only server piece is the existing sign-in helper, which keeps nothing.
7. As a user, the app can only write the answer and steer forms. It can't write agent records, approvals or anything else, and it never sends a write I didn't confirm.
8. As a user, a write that fails or whose result is unknown says so plainly, and a retry never posts a second copy without asking.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Where:** everything is in `openwizdev/WizSite` under `app/`, tested in WizSite's CI. The tickets live in this tracker.
- **Contract first.** One WizSite contract, `contracts/app-records.v1.md`, fixes: each card action and the exact comment it writes; the records layer's browser interface (`OW.records`); the card interface the queue renders through (`OW.cards.decision`, `OW.cards.spec`); the queue item shapes; and the v2 switch. Its fixtures are the comment bodies the tests compare byte for byte.
- **Decision answers** use decisions.v1's contextual answer framing (`openwiz decision answer v1`, a compact context line, a blank line, then the verbatim answer segment), posted as a comment on the request's own subject. Yes is the answer segment the contract gives for the shown Rec. No and typed replies are own-words answers, kept byte for byte. `live`, `release` and `publish` risks confirm twice, as the contract says. `unknown` risk, a stale or superseded request, or an unreadable record can't be answered.
- **Spec steers** are comments on the spec in the steer words launch-fleet's steer reference reads: Not now is `stop`, Change something is the owner's typed words, verbatim, and Ship it is the contract's fixed go-on steer. The contract cites each source form.
- **One records layer** (`app/records.js`) composes, previews and posts. It is the only code that sends a write. `data.js`'s request guard allows exactly one write: `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}/comments` on the picked repository, and only through the layer. The layer refuses to compose any other form, including agent records (`launch-fleet:` lines, decisions.v1 request records, machine or human plan approvals and late-look records).
- **Dry run.** Each action first returns the exact comment body, its target and its public visibility. Posting needs a separate confirm of that same preview. A dry-run mode posts nothing at all.
- **One send.** Each preview carries an operation id. Retry, reload and double taps reuse it. Before re-posting after an unknown outcome, the layer reads the subject's comments for that exact body.
- **Sign-in.** The token stays in the browser's storage, as it does today. The sign-in helper in `functions/` stays keep-nothing and gains no route. The OpenWiz Viewer GitHub App needs Issues: read and write, so it can post comments as the user. Pull requests stay read-only.
- **Switch.** The queue and its writes are off by default. A per-browser switch turns them on for the owner's room. Turning them on for everyone is this spec's last ticket.

## Testing Decisions

- **Seams:** the records layer is tested in Node against the contract's fixtures, showing the exact bodies, the refusals and the request guard. The queue and both cards are tested in a headless browser against recorded GitHub answers, in the same way `scripts/app-check.mjs` already tests the v1 app.
- Every test proves its claim red first: the check fails before the change and passes after.
- **Security review:** the records layer and write-path ticket gets a full review, security included. That covers token handling and storage, the request guard, the refused forms, injection through own words (the answer segment is never parsed), the preview matching what is posted, and no server piece holding a token.

## Proof

| Claim | Proof |
| --- | --- |
| Each action writes exactly the contract's comment | Node tests compare composed bodies byte for byte with the fixtures |
| Only the answer and steer forms can be written | Node tests: every agent-record form and every other method or URL is refused |
| Nothing posts without a confirmed preview | Browser tests: dry run shows the body and sends no request; confirm sends exactly one |
| One queue, two kinds of card | Browser test against recorded answers: decision and spec cards in one ordered queue |
| A spec card shows its video, else its plan picture | Browser test with one spec of each kind |
| The token never leaves the browser except to GitHub | Review, plus a test that the sign-in helper's routes and answers are unchanged |
| It works in the owner's room | Live check: the owner answers one real decision and steers one real spec from the app, and each comment reads back in the contract's form |

## Checkpoints

- One-way door: yes
- User-visible: yes

## Live check

In the owner's own room, with the switch on: answer one real open decision and steer one real spec from the app. The orchestrator reads back each comment's author, subject and exact body against the contract. Only then does the last ticket turn v2 on for everyone.

## Out of Scope

- The Ideas page, where a grill starts per idea from the app. It waits for v3.
- Moving records off GitHub. That isn't decided, and the records layer only keeps the door open.
- Any backend, database or new server route.
- Changing how the orchestrator or fleets act on an answer. v2 writes the forms they read; whether a comment counts as the owner's word keeps its existing rules.
- Acting on app comments automatically: that waits for openwizdev/openwiz#1402. Until then the orchestrator reads them as the owner's answers.

## Further Notes

Planned from the confirmed App v2 grill (2026-11-22). The confirmation is a private record, and the machine plan approval links it. The spec's video goes in a comment, not here.

## Parent

## What to build

A fleet wake reads a spec, its tickets and their pull requests' states in one GraphQL query (paged), within GraphQL's own 5,000 points, instead of REST lists and searches.

Keep #2376's repository keys for closing pull requests.

**Relies on:** nothing

## Links

## Acceptance criteria
